rules.statement: Define a failure-code vocabulary as a `public static class` of `public const string` snake_case values, never as an enum, so that a custom handler can supply a code of its own.
rules.why: Failure vocabularies are open: an enum would shut out codes that extension points such as custom validation handlers name.
rules.check: Look for new failure-kind enums, or code properties typed as an enum, where callers or extensions might need to add their own values. Also check that constant values are snake_case strings.

rules.statement: Set a failure's machine-readable code at the point where the failure is detected, and have the layers above pass it through unchanged instead of translating it with a hard-coded mapping table.
rules.why: A mapping table between two vocabularies loses any code it doesn't list, including codes that custom handlers name.
rules.check: Look for switch statements or dictionaries that translate one layer's failure codes into another's, and for wrapping code that drops the inner code or replaces it with a generic one.

rules.statement: When a higher-level failure vocabulary shares codes with a lower-level one, alias each shared constant to the lower-level constant (`= LowerCodes.X`) instead of repeating the string literal.
rules.why: Each code string is then defined once, so the two vocabularies can't drift apart.
rules.check: Look for duplicated string literals across failure-code classes where the higher-level assembly references the lower-level one.

rules.statement: Code that acts on why an operation failed must branch on the failure's machine-readable code, never on the text of its message or reason.
rules.why: The reason text is meant for humans and logs. It isn't a stable contract, and callers need to tell one failure from another without matching text.
rules.check: Look for `Message.Contains`, string comparisons or regex matches on exception messages or failure-reason text that decide control flow or map to error names.

rules.statement: A JWT validation requirement or handler that fails must record a specific failure code together with its reason (for example `Fail(code, reason)`), and a custom assertion that needs its own code must record it before it returns `false`.
rules.why: The validator joins every handler failure into one exception, so a failed requirement needs a code that callers can read. Without one it falls back to a generic code.
rules.check: Look at new or changed validation handlers, requirements and assertions: each failure path should call `Fail` with a code from the failure-code vocabulary (or a custom one), not record only reason text.

rules.statement: A claim-value requirement must declare its failure code explicitly (for example `invalid_issuer` or `invalid_audience`) rather than have the code inferred from the claim name it checks.
rules.why: A declared code is explicit and stable. Inferring it from a claim name is implicit and breaks for custom requirements.
rules.check: Look for logic that derives a failure code from a claim name (for example `iss` → `invalid_issuer`) instead of reading the requirement's own `FailureCode` setting.

rules.statement: Don't re-check `iss`, `aud`, `exp`, `nbf` or other validated claims outside the JWT validator to work out which check failed. Read the validation result's failure code instead.
rules.why: Re-checking duplicates the validator's requirements and bounds a token's lifetime outside the lifetime requirement, which the conventions forbid.
rules.check: Look for code after a failed JWT validation that parses the token's claims and compares the issuer, audience or timestamps again.

rules.statement: A token validation failure reason must never include the token itself or any part of it.
rules.why: Failure reasons are logged and shown as human-readable text, and putting the token in them would leak a credential.
rules.check: Look for failure reasons, exception messages or log templates that interpolate the raw token, its encoded segments or the full payload.

rules.statement: In a validation result type, derive success from the failure code (`IsValid => FailureCode is null`) and resolve the default code for unrecognized exceptions in one place, not with a separate success flag or scattered fallbacks.
rules.why: With one source of truth, validity and the failure code can't disagree, and the fallback code lives in one place.
rules.check: Look for result types that store a separate `IsValid` boolean next to a failure code, or for callers that each supply their own fallback code when an exception carries none.
